Reliable broadcast lets one designated party, the broadcaster, hand a value to nnn parties so that the honest ones end up agreeing on it, even when up to fff of them are Byzantine, meaning they can behave arbitrarily. DAG-based consensus protocols run one broadcast instance per block per round. Every step a broadcast takes therefore shows up in commit latency, and every step by which one honest party can lag behind another shows up in how long timeouts must be.
The paper by Nikita Polianskii (IOTA Foundation) asks what it costs to make signature-free reliable broadcast fast in the common case. It proves that, for 3f+1≤n<4f3f+1 \le n < 4f3f+1≤n<4f, any deterministic protocol that delivers in two steps whenever at most n−3fn-3fn−3f parties are faulty must let honest deliveries spread over at least three steps. It then gives two protocols. Confirm/ack keeps the largest possible optimistic fault budget across the whole range and reaches latencies (2, 3, 4). Paired witnesses reach (2, 3, 3), which matches the lower bound over a stated parameter range. The paper’s summary is that, in the matching range, maximal optimism costs exactly one totality step relative to Bracha’s classic protocol and no step of good-case latency.
Reliable broadcast and its three clocksThe paper’s model has n≥3f+1n \ge 3f+1n≥3f+1 parties, one of them the broadcaster. An adaptive adversary can corrupt up to fff parties during the execution; a party is honest if it is never corrupted. Parties communicate over pairwise authenticated channels: a receiver knows who sent a message, but cannot prove to a third party what it received. There are no signatures, no trusted setup, and no correlated state carried from earlier instances. Messages between honest parties are eventually delivered, in any order.
A protocol is a reliable broadcast protocol if it satisfies three properties. Validity: with an honest broadcaster, every honest party eventually delivers the broadcaster’s value and nothing else. Agreement: no two honest parties deliver different values. Totality: if any honest party delivers, every honest party eventually delivers. Totality is what makes a locally delivered value safe to act on inside a larger protocol, because a party knows the others will catch up.
Latency is measured in steps, where one step is δ\deltaδ, the actual delay bound on messages between honest parties in a given execution. The protocol is not told δ\deltaδ; a latency bound must hold for every δ>0\delta > 0δ>0. The paper writes latency as a triple (do,ds,dt)(d_o, d_s, d_t)(do​,ds​,dt​):
dsd_sds​, the good-case latency, is the worst time from an honest broadcaster’s invocation until all honest parties have delivered, over executions with up to fff Byzantine parties. dod_odo​, the optimistic good-case latency with budget bbb, is the same quantity restricted to executions with at most bbb Byzantine parties, for an optimistic fault budget b≤fb \le fb≤f. dtd_tdt​, the totality delay, is the supremum over all executions, with any broadcaster, of the time from the first honest delivery to the last. This is the elapsed convention of Yu et al. (2026). The paper also splits totality into dtHd_t^HdtH​ and dtBd_t^BdtB​, the totality delay restricted to honest and Byzantine broadcasters, with dt=max⁡{dtH,dtB}d_t = \max\{d_t^H, d_t^B\}dt​=max{dtH​,dtB​}. Since every honest-broadcaster delivery happens between invocation and the good-case deadline, dtH≤dsd_t^H \le d_sdtH​≤ds​ always holds.
Bracha’s 1987 protocol is the reference point. The broadcaster proposes, parties echo the proposal, a party sends ready after enough echoes or after f+1f+1f+1 readies, and delivers after 2f+12f+12f+1 readies. It is (3, 3, 2): three steps in the good case, and once an honest party delivers, its quorum contains f+1f+1f+1 honest readies that reach everyone within a step, trigger relayed readies, and complete delivery within a second step. The paper points out that an early first delivery does not shrink this to one step under nonuniform delays: the honest readies in the early quorum still take a full step to reach others, and the readies they trigger take a second.
The price Opt-RBC pays for two-step deliveryAbraham, Ren, and Xiang (2021) showed that two-step delivery under all fff faults requires n≥4fn \ge 4fn≥4f without signatures. Shrestha et al. (2025) relaxed the goal: deliver in two steps only when at most bbb parties are actually Byzantine, and fall back to slower delivery otherwise. For 3f+1≤n<4f3f+1 \le n < 4f3f+1≤n<4f they showed the largest feasible budget is
b∗=⌊n/2⌋−f. b^* = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - f. b∗=⌊n/2⌋−f.Their protocol, Opt-RBC, attains this budget. The paper uses the corrected arXiv v4 of May 2026, which adds an acknowledgment layer to fix a termination issue in the earlier CCS 2025 version. In the paper’s convention Opt-RBC is (2, 4, 4): good-case latency rises from Bracha’s three steps to four, and totality delay from two to four. Shrestha et al. report a bad-case latency of five, but that is measured from invocation; four is the elapsed first-to-last figure. A superseded v2 of their paper had claimed two-step optimism together with a three-step good case.
The paper’s question is whether this price is necessary: can maximal optimism coexist with Bracha’s three-step good case, and with his two-step totality? The stakes come from consensus. In protocols that disseminate blocks by reliable broadcast, good-case latency controls how quickly honest proposals become available, and totality controls how quickly the other honest parties catch up once one delivers. When the same delivered evidence drives round advancement, totality also bounds how far apart parties enter rounds, which sizes recovery timers.
A lower bound: early fast delivery imposes a deadlineTheorem 1.1 states: let 3f+1≤n<4f3f+1 \le n < 4f3f+1≤n<4f and n−3f≤b≤⌊n/2⌋−fn - 3f \le b \le \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - fn−3f≤b≤⌊n/2⌋−f. In the paper’s deterministic model, every reliable broadcast protocol with two-step honest-broadcaster delivery under at most bbb faults has totality delay at least three. This already holds over executions with an honest broadcaster and at most fff faulty non-broadcasters. For n≤4f−2n \le 4f-2n≤4f−2, the bound also holds when only non-broadcasters are required to deliver and only their deliveries count toward the totality clock.
The theorem quantifies over very general protocols: arbitrary messages, recipient-specific packets, timers, repeated sends, continued communication after delivery, and parties that read real time. It does not assume threshold rules, bounded message complexity, or a three-step good case. It does not cover randomized protocols, or protocols that are given the actual delay bound. Because the proof uses only static fault sets, it also applies to protocols that tolerate adaptive corruption.
In plain words: if a protocol promises two-step delivery even when as few as n−3fn-3fn−3f parties are faulty, then some honest-broadcaster execution has one honest party delivering very early while another has to wait almost three steps. At n=3f+1n = 3f+1n=3f+1, n−3f=1n - 3f = 1n−3f=1, so even a budget of one fault already costs the extra totality step. Since dtH≤dsd_t^H \le d_sdtH​≤ds​, a protocol with ds=3d_s = 3ds​=3 cannot do worse than three on honest-broadcaster spread, so the bound is tight for such protocols; it says nothing about dtBd_t^BdtB​, which could still be two.
The partition behind the proofThe proof splits the parties into five groups. With s=n−3f−1s = n - 3f - 1s=n−3f−1, which lies between 0 and f−2f-2f−2 in this range, there is a source group S\mathcal{S}S of size f−s−1f - s - 1f−s−1 containing the broadcaster, two endpoint groups EA,EBE_A, E_BEA​,EB​ of size s+1s+1s+1, and two common groups KA,KBK_A, K_BKA​,KB​ of size fff. An anchor party hhh is chosen inside S\mathcal{S}S as an ordinary recipient when S\mathcal{S}S has at least two members; otherwise hhh is the broadcaster itself, which happens only at n=4f−1n = 4f-1n=4f−1 and is the case that needs the convention that the broadcaster’s own delivery starts the totality clock. How the six executions of the lower bound pass deliveries and identical histories from one to the next. The fast executions FAF_AFA​ and FBF_BFB​ have the broadcaster input AAA or BBB, all delays equal to ε\varepsilonε, and one endpoint group faulty and silent after its initial packets. That is s+1≤bs+1 \le bs+1≤b faults, so two-step optimism forces the honest anchor hhh to deliver by 2ε2\varepsilon2ε.
The forcing executions XAX_AXA​ and XBX_BXB​ keep the anchor’s view identical to the fast execution through 2ε2\varepsilon2ε while slowing everything else down. In XAX_AXA​, the group EBE_BEB​ is now honest but late: it receives every initial packet only at η\etaη. Other honest messages take η\etaη, except that messages sent to hhh by time ε\varepsilonε still arrive after ε\varepsilonε (the anchor exception), and the faulty KBK_BKB​ replays its fast-execution packets to hhh. The bridges WAW_AWA​ and WBW_BWB​ have a Byzantine broadcaster. In WAW_AWA​, the faulty members of S\mathcal{S}S send their XAX_AXA​ streams toward the AAA side and their XBX_BXB​ streams toward KBK_BKB​. The faulty EBE_BEB​ copies, under its own identity, the stream that honest EBE_BEB​ sends in WBW_BWB​ toward the common groups, and copies the late group’s stream from XAX_AXA​ toward EAE_AEA​. Nontransferable authentication is what permits this copying. The four executions are constructed jointly by increasing time, and every copied packet copies an honest packet sent at least ε\varepsilonε before its arrival, so the construction is not circular.
Two lemmas carry the proof. Lemma 3.1 (causal cut) says that the complete timed histories of KAK_AKA​ agree in XAX_AXA​ and WAW_AWA​ before 2η2\eta2η, and those of EAE_AEA​ agree before 3η3\eta3η, with the mirror statements on the BBB side. The reason is a sender-by-sender comparison: the late group sends nothing noninitial before η\etaη, so its first such packet reaches KAK_AKA​ no earlier than 2η2\eta2η; in WAW_AWA​ the copied stream is silent before JJJ apart from matching initial packets; S\mathcal{S}S and KBK_BKB​ are copied explicitly; and packets from EAE_AEA​ or within KAK_AKA​ arriving before 2η2\eta2η were sent from strictly earlier, already matching histories. A packet from KAK_AKA​ arriving at EAE_AEA​ before 3η3\eta3η was sent before 2η2\eta2η, inside the interval just established.
Lemma 3.2 (common indistinguishability) says every party in KA∪KBK_A \cup K_BKA​∪KB​ has the same complete history in WAW_AWA​ and WBW_BWB​ for all time. Each member of S\mathcal{S}S sends the same streams to the common groups in both bridges, each endpoint identity is honest in one bridge and an exact Byzantine copy in the other, and common-to-common traffic is identical by induction. The private EAE_AEA​–EBE_BEB​ streams differ, but each such channel has a Byzantine end in each bridge.
The contradiction follows. Since H<3ηH < 3\etaH<3η, the causal cut carries the forced delivery of AAA by EAE_AEA​ into WAW_AWA​, and of BBB by EBE_BEB​ into WBW_BWB​. Both bridges are fair asynchronous executions, with honest delays at most JJJ, so totality and agreement apply even though the hypothesis about DDD does not. Totality forces the common parties to deliver, agreement forces AAA in WAW_AWA​ and BBB in WBW_BWB​, and identical deterministic histories make that impossible.
The author places this argument in the line of four-execution indistinguishability proofs by Abraham, Ren, and Xiang and by Shrestha et al. What is new is preserving an early delivery under nonuniform larger delays, fixing the resulting deadline across the history comparisons, and using only eventual totality in the bridges. The source group generalizes the padding set of size at most one in Shrestha et al.’s proof, which is what lowers the fast executions’ fault count to n−3fn - 3fn−3f. The construction needs n≤3f+bn \le 3f + bn≤3f+b, because the common groups total at most 2f2f2f, S∪EA\mathcal{S} \cup E_AS∪EA​ is faulty in a bridge, and EBE_BEB​ is faulty in a fast execution. The paper stresses that this is a limit of the partition, not a proof that smaller budgets escape the bound. At n=4fn = 4fn=4f the source group would be empty although it must contain the broadcaster.
Paired witnesses: binding a confirm to its author’s echoThe construction fixes f≥2f \ge 2f≥2, n=3f+1+sn = 3f + 1 + sn=3f+1+s, and a budget in the range
1≤b≤min⁡{f,⌊n/2⌋−f,2s+3}. 1 \le b \le \min\{f, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - f, 2s+3\}. 1≤b≤min{f,⌊n/2⌋−f,2s+3}.Let N=n−1N = n - 1N=n−1 be the number of non-broadcasters. Only non-broadcasters send echo, vote, confirm, and witness messages; every party, including the broadcaster, can send ready and deliver. Each party sends each message type at most once per instance, across all values, and keeps processing after it delivers. A receiver keeps one slot per message type and author: it is filled by the first such message and never changed. Every quorum is therefore a set of distinct authors, and a Byzantine party can appear in quorums for different values at different receivers, but cannot stand in for another party.
Figure 3 shows the message flow. A label on an arrow is the number of distinct authors that triggers the next message, and the gray text marks the three delivery rules. There are two ways from echo to ready, through vote below and through confirm and witness above, and neither passes through an acknowledgment.

Confirm also requires the author’s own echo. With an honest broadcaster every honest party has QQQ echoes after two steps when at most bbb parties are Byzantine, and CCC confirms after three. The witness message instead certifies, at its author, PPP identities whose echo slot and confirm slot both hold vvv. A claim by another party to have seen such a pair does not count; only the receiver’s own slots do. Because echo slots are immutable, a paired author’s echo for vvv can never later turn into an echo for another value at that receiver.

Delivery and catch-up within three stepsLemma 4.3 gives the latencies. With an honest broadcaster, everyone has the proposal by step one. With at most bbb faults, QQQ honest echoes arrive by step two; with up to fff, CCC honest echoes arrive by step two and CCC honest confirms by step three. These finite message chains also prove eventual totality without any delay bound.
Theorem 1.2 collects the result: under the budget range above, there is a signature-free asynchronous reliable broadcast protocol against adaptive corruption of at most fff parties with optimistic latency two under at most bbb faults, good-case latency three, and totality delay at most three. At most 5(n−1)2+2(n−1)5(n-1)^2 + 2(n-1)5(n−1)2+2(n−1) messages are sent while their authors are uncorrupted, including after delivery, since each non-broadcaster sends at most five multicasts and the broadcaster at most two. It quantifies over arbitrary deterministic protocols, with timers and any message format, and it says that at n=3f+1n = 3f+1n=3f+1 a fast path that tolerates even one fault costs a step of catch-up. That closes a question a protocol designer would otherwise keep trying to engineer around.
The constructions I read with more caution, and the paper supplies the reasons. Opt-RBC needed a corrected version to fix termination. Two natural variants of confirm/ack break totality at ten parties. Proposition B.2 shows that the paired-witness rules, unchanged, lose totality as soon as the budget is one above 2s+32s+32s+3, first at 22 parties. When we built the BFT orderer for Fabric we gave up pipelining to keep the view change simple enough to trust. A broadcast with six message types, whose safety turns on thresholds one apart, is the opposite choice. I would want it model-checked. I would also want the configuration code to refuse a budget outside the proven range, including after a membership change moves nnn.
For the committee sizes I worked with, the interesting result is the plain one. At 7 parties and f=2f = 2f=2 the largest budget is one, and the paper says Bracha with fast echo delivery already reaches (2, 3, 3) there with three message types. Paired witnesses start to matter from f=3f = 3f=3.
The paper compares against Opt-RBC, and there paired witnesses are never worse on any row of Table 4. Against Bracha the same table is mixed. Good-case commit is 4 steps for both. Paired witnesses gain a step only when at most bbb parties are faulty, and they pay for it in every execution: the Simple-IT round timer goes from 5Δ5\Delta5Δ to 6Δ6\Delta6Δ. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how often a deployment runs with no more than bbb faulty parties, and nothing here measures it. The consensus rows are substitutions into other papers’ formulas, as the author says.
Two things would decide adoption for me. The first is state. A party cannot drop an instance at delivery and gets no bound on when it can, and a DAG runs one instance per block. The second is evidence. Channels are authenticated but nothing is transferable, so a delivered value cannot be shown to anyone outside the instance. In Fabric a block carries a quorum of orderer signatures so that a peer can check it without trusting whoever sent it. The paper notes that an interface needing transferable certificates requires a separate argument. For a permissioned ledger that argument is most of the work.
Optimistic Reliable Broadcast in Three Steps. Nikita Polianskii. arXiv, 2026.
summary: Reliable broadcast lets one designated party, the broadcaster, hand a value to nnn parties so that the honest ones end up agreeing on it, even when up to fff of them are Byzantine, meaning they can behave arbitrarily. DAG-based consensus protocols run one broadcast instance per block per round. Every step a broadcast takes therefore shows up in commit latency, and every step by which one honest party can lag behind another shows up in how long timeouts must be.
title: Two-step optimism, three-step totality: paired witnesses for reliable broadcast

content:
For most of the last decade, work on fast Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus has focused on one number: message complexity, meaning how many protocol messages the validators exchange per decision. HotStuff (Yin et al., 2019) brought that number down to linear in the partially synchronous setting by routing all votes through a leader. The paper by Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino and Spiegelman, published at EuroSys 2022, argues that this target misses where the cost actually sits in a real ledger. The expensive part is not agreeing on an order. It is moving the transactions themselves to every validator, reliably.
The authors build two systems around that claim. Narwhal is a mempool, the layer that collects and spreads pending transactions, redesigned as a round-based directed acyclic graph (DAG) of certified blocks. Tusk is an asynchronous consensus protocol that orders that DAG without sending a single extra message. On a wide-area network, the paper reports that HotStuff running over Narwhal reaches over 130,000 transactions per second at under 2 seconds of latency, against 1,800 tx/s for a conventional HotStuff deployment, and that adding worker machines per validator pushes throughput to about 600,000 tx/s with no increase in latency.
Why message complexity is the wrong thing to minimizeThe paper opens with two observations about leader-based protocols. First, a protocol that minimizes total message count by funneling everything through a leader concentrates load on that leader, which becomes the bottleneck. Second, message complexity counts metadata: votes, signatures and hashes on the order of 100 bytes. Blocks of transactions are on the order of 10 MB. For committees up to roughly 50 nodes, the asymptotic difference between linear and quadratic metadata is dwarfed by the cost of shipping bulk data.
There is also a structural point. In ledgers like Bitcoin or LibraBFT (now DiemBFT), clients send transactions to a validator, a gossip mempool spreads them around, and then the leader re-sends a subset of them inside a consensus proposal. Transactions cross the network twice, and the second crossing sits on the critical path of consensus.
The paper states its hypothesis directly: a better mempool, one that reliably distributes transactions, is the key enabler of a high-performance ledger. It should be separated from consensus altogether, leaving consensus only the job of ordering small fixed-size references. If this is right, system throughput should be largely unaffected by consensus throughput, and different consensus protocols layered on top should differ mainly in latency.
Earlier systems such as Prism (Bagaria et al., 2019) and work on PBFT-style batching already separated large payloads from metadata. The authors’ criticism is that they did so without guaranteeing reliability: they work well with no faults and degrade badly at the first network hiccup. To test this, the authors build Batched-HS, a HotStuff variant where validators broadcast batches and the leader proposes only their hashes. It serves as the representative of that prior approach throughout the evaluation.
The mempool as a certified key-value storeNarwhal is specified as an abstraction before it is described as a protocol. The model is a message-passing system of nnn parties, a computationally bounded adversary that controls the network and can corrupt up to f<n/3f < n/3f<n/3 parties, and asynchronous eventually reliable links: no bound on delay, and a finite but unknown number of lost messages.
A block bbb contains a list of transactions and a list of references to earlier blocks. Its cryptographic digest ddd serves as its identifier. A reference from bbb to b′b'b′ encodes a happened-before relation, written b′→bb' \to bb′→b, and by convention all referenced blocks happen before all transactions in the block.
The abstraction offers four operations. write(d,b)\mathrm{write}(d, b)write(d,b) stores a block and returns c(d)c(d)c(d), an unforgeable certificate of availability; the write succeeds when the certificate forms. valid(d,c(d))\mathrm{valid}(d, c(d))valid(d,c(d)) checks a certificate. read(d)\mathrm{read}(d)read(d) returns the block. read_causal(d)\mathrm{read\_causal}(d)read_causal(d) returns the set BBB of all blocks with a transitive happened-before path to the block with digest ddd.
Narwhal guarantees five properties:
Integrity: for any certified digest ddd, any two honest reads that return a value return the same value. Block-Availability: if an honest party invokes read(d)\mathrm{read}(d)read(d) after write(d,b)\mathrm{write}(d,b)write(d,b) has succeeded, the read eventually returns bbb. Containment: if BBB is returned by read_causal(d)\mathrm{read\_causal}(d)read_causal(d), then for every b′∈Bb' \in Bb′∈B, the set B′B'B′ returned by read_causal(d′)\mathrm{read\_causal}(d')read_causal(d′) satisfies B′⊆BB' \subseteq BB′⊆B. 2/3-Causality: read_causal(d)\mathrm{read\_causal}(d)read_causal(d) returns at least 2/3 of the blocks written successfully before write(d,b)\mathrm{write}(d,b)write(d,b) was invoked. 1/2-Chain Quality: at least half of the blocks in a returned causal set were written by honest parties. Each property has a job. Integrity and Block-Availability let consensus order only short certificates, since the content behind them is guaranteed to exist and be unique. Causality and Containment mean that once consensus agrees on one digest, everything it causally depends on can be ordered too, including blocks produced while consensus was stalled. Chain Quality is what gives censorship resistance. The authors also add a non-theoretical goal, scale-out: throughput should grow linearly with the resources each validator commits, without hurting latency.
Five steps from gossip to NarwhalThe paper motivates the design by evolving a plain gossip mempool in five steps.
Step one broadcasts blocks rather than individual transactions and lets the leader propose a block hash. This removes the double transmission, but validators must still download a block before they can vouch for its hash, and that download is on the critical path.
Step two consistently broadcasts each block so that it produces a certificate proving the block will be available. The leader proposes certificates. The remaining problem is that every mempool block needs its own certificate in the proposal, and if consensus loses liveness for a while, the backlog of certificates to commit grows without bound.
Step three adds causality. Mempool blocks include certificates of earlier mempool blocks from all validators, so one certificate stands for a block and its entire causal history. A leader proposing one fixed-size certificate thereby proposes an extension of the sequence covering everything in that history. Consensus delays now cost latency but not average throughput, since blocks keep being produced and are committed later in bulk.
Two issues remain at this stage: a very fast validator could flood others with blocks they must download, and slow honest validators might never get their blocks referenced. Step four imposes rounds. Each block carries a round number and must include a quorum of certificates from the previous round. A validator cannot outrun the honest majority, and every proposal necessarily contains a fraction of honest blocks. The authors claim this makes Narwhal-HotStuff the only partially synchronous quorum-based protocol with censorship resistance in the sense of HoneyBadgerBFT (Miller et al., 2016), without threshold encryption: an adversary gains nothing by killing leaders whose proposals it dislikes, because every proposal includes at least 50% honest content.
Step five splits each validator into one primary and many workers, which handle batches of transactions while the primary handles only hashes. This is the scale-out step.
Rounds, certificates and the block DAGEach validator keeps a local round rrr, starting at zero. It accumulates client transactions into a transaction list and certificates for round r−1r-1r−1 into a certificate list. Once it holds certificates from 2f+12f+12f+1 distinct validators for round r−1r-1r−1, it advances to round rrr and broadcasts a new block containing its identity, the round number, its pending transactions, the round r−1r-1r−1 certificates, and its signature. Correct validators create one block per round.
Figure 1 is the paper’s picture of three rounds of this process with four validators, so f=1f=1f=1. Each stack in a Blocks column is one validator’s block for that round, and the shaded slot in it is the block’s certificate list. Follow the arrows out of that slot: each points to a certificate of the previous round, and there are 2f+1=32f+1 = 32f+1=3 of them. The short arrow from a certificate points back to the block it certifies. In round rrr only three of the four blocks have a certificate so far, and that is enough for every validator to build its block for round r+1r+1r+1. The lower part of the figure lists what a block and a certificate contain.
Figure 1. Three rounds of Narwhal. In round r−1r-1r−1 there are enough (N−fN-fN−f) certified blocks, and validators start building blocks for round rrr. Each includes a batch of transactions and N−fN-fN−f certificates for round r−1r-1r−1. Blocks for rrr can only include certificates from the previous round. Once a validator has a ready block it broadcasts it to others to form a certificate and then shares the certificate with all other validators to include at round r+1r+1r+1.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 2 (© the authors) Other validators check the block and, if it is valid, store it and reply with a signature over its digest, round and creator. A block is valid if it carries a valid creator signature, is at the checker’s current round, is either a round-0 genesis block or contains at least 2f+12f+12f+1 certificates from round r−1r-1r−1, and is the first block received from that creator for round rrr. A block from a future round carries the 2f+12f+12f+1 certificates that let the checker advance its own round and then sign. When the creator collects 2f+12f+12f+1 signatures, it combines them into a certificate of availability and sends that certificate to everyone, who will reference it in round r+1r+1r+1.
The exchange for one block is two messages out and one back, drawn as a sequence diagram in Figure 2. The block exists as soon as validator A sends it, but nobody may reference it until the certificate comes back around.

How a block becomes a certificate of availability: the messages of validator A in one round. The security intuition is quorum intersection. A certificate has 2f+12f+12f+1 signatures, so at least f+1f+1f+1 honest validators checked and stored the block: it can always be fetched. Since honest validators sign only one block per creator per round, two conflicting blocks for the same slot can never both gather 2f+12f+12f+1 signatures, which prevents equivocation. Because each block references certificates from the previous round, induction shows every block in a certified block’s causal history is itself certified and available.
The appendix turns this into proofs. Integrity follows from collision resistance of the hash. Block-Availability follows because at least f+1f+1f+1 honest validators store each certified block, and a read that waits for n−fn-fn−f replies reaches at least one of them. Chain Quality follows because each round in a causal history contains at least 2f+12f+12f+1 blocks, of which at most fff are Byzantine. Causality follows because each round has at most 3f+13f+13f+1 written blocks and a causal history picks up at least 2f+12f+12f+1 of them. Containment follows because uniqueness of certified blocks per creator and round means all honest validators agree on the references inside every certified block, and this applies recursively.
Putting HotStuff on topNarwhal can be used in two ways: an existing consensus protocol orders Narwhal’s certificates, or the DAG itself is read as a consensus protocol once a random coin is added. Figure 3 shows both, separated by the dashed line. In the first, a partially synchronous protocol such as HotStuff or LibraBFT runs on top. Instead of proposing a block of transactions, the leader proposes one or more Narwhal certificates. When a certificate commits, its full uncommitted causal history is ordered by a deterministic rule. Since Narwhal guarantees that everyone sees the same causal history for a given certificate, every validator derives the same total order.
Figure 3. Any consensus protocol can execute over the mempool by occasionally ordering certificates to Narwhal blocks. Narwhal guarantees their availability for the SMR execution. Alternatively, Narwhal structure can be interpreted as an asynchronous consensus protocol with the (zero-message cost) addition of a random-coin.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 3 (© the authors) The paper lists two gains. Without faults, a leader broadcasting transactions saturates its own bandwidth while others sit idle; Narwhal spreads the bulk transfer evenly. During asynchrony or under a Byzantine leader, a partially synchronous protocol makes no progress, and with a naive mempool throughput drops to zero. Narwhal keeps certifying blocks at full speed regardless, and the next successful commit sweeps up everything produced in the meantime. Latency still suffers during those periods, which is the gap Tusk is designed to close.
The paper summarizes the theory in a comparison table, with latency counted in round trips or certificates. In the average case, HotStuff takes 3, Narwhal-HotStuff 4 and Tusk 4.5. With fff crashed leaders, both HotStuff variants have O(n)O(n)O(n) worst-case latency while Tusk stays at 4.5. Under asynchrony, only Tusk has bounded latency, 7. On an unstable network that allows one commit between asynchronous periods, Narwhal-HotStuff and Tusk keep synchrony-level throughput while HotStuff does not; under full asynchrony, only Tusk does.
Garbage collection with fixed memoryThe authors present garbage collection as a theoretical contribution, since it has been a roadblock for DAG-based protocols such as Hashgraph (Baird, 2016). A DAG is a local structure that converges across validators eventually but with no time bound, so validators may need to retain all history to help peers catch up and to validate arbitrarily old messages. A footnote records that a garbage collection bug in their own implementation consumed 120 GB of RAM within minutes, against a normal footprint of 700 MB.
Narwhal’s round structure solves the validation side: deciding whether to sign a block requires only knowledge of the current round, and a certified block can be checked with verification keys alone. The remaining danger is that two validators garbage-collect different rounds and so disagree on the causal history of a newly committed block. Narwhal therefore uses the consensus layer to agree on the garbage collection round. Older blocks can be moved off the validator, and older messages ignored.
If an adversary delays a block until it is collected, the honest node that created it re-injects its transactions into a later block. Individual DAG blocks may be censored, but every transaction is eventually included, and by 1/2-Chain Quality enters the consensus output within a constant number of rounds. The upshot is O(n)O(n)O(n) in-memory state per validator, covering the current round. Older certified blocks can be served by a passive store or a content distribution network, since certificates already guarantee their integrity.
Reliable broadcast without perfect linksTextbook reliable broadcast, such as double-echo, assumes perfect point-to-point links that retransmit forever, which requires unbounded application memory. TCP drops all state when a connection breaks, and acknowledgments do not help against Byzantine peers who never send them.
Narwhal relies on its quorums instead. Once a validator moves to round r+1r+1r+1, it stops retransmitting and drops all undelivered messages for earlier rounds. A certificate by itself does not give the totality property of reliable broadcast, since some honest nodes may have the block and others not. But when a validator receives a certified block for round r+1r+1r+1, it can pull every missing block in its causal history from the signers of the corresponding certificates. Since at least f+1f+1f+1 honest validators store each block, the probability of a correct reply grows exponentially with the number of validators asked. Only O(1)O(1)O(1) requests per block are active at a time, O(1)O(1)O(1) on average suffice, and an adversary attacking links can force at most O(n)O(n)O(n), which matches the worst-case lower bound of Dolev and Reischuk (1985). Retransmission storage is bounded by O(n)O(n)O(n).
Primaries, workers and streaming batchesAny mempool is ultimately bounded by what a single validator can receive and store. The paper’s observation is that a validator is a unit of trust, not a single computer. Each validator becomes one primary machine and several worker machines. Figure 4 is the paper’s drawing of one round with four validators, one per row, and three workers each. Every worker produces batches, the three batches of a validator feed the primary block to their right, and the block gets its certificate in the last column. The dotted vertical lines join the corresponding workers of the four validators.
Figure 4. Scale-Out Architecture in Narwhal. Within each validator, there is one primary machine that handles the meta-data of building the DAG and multiple worker machines (3 shown in the example) each one streaming Transactions batches to other validators. The hashes of the batches are sent to the primary that includes them in the next block. Clients send transactions to worker machines at all validators.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 4 (© the authors) Figure 4 shows the data structures and leaves the messages implicit. Figure 5 draws them for two validators with two workers each. The thing to look at is which links cross the validator boundary: transaction data moves only between workers, and the primaries exchange blocks, signatures and certificates that contain nothing larger than a hash.

Two validators, each split into a primary and two workers, and what travels on each link. A load balancer spreads incoming transactions across workers. Each worker forms batches, sends them to the matching worker at every other validator, and after a quorum acknowledges, hands the batch hash to its primary. The primary runs Narwhal unchanged, except that its blocks contain batch hashes instead of transactions, and it signs another validator’s block only once its own workers have stored the referenced batches. By induction, everything under a certificate remains retrievable. Missing batches are pulled worker to worker at the primary’s instruction, and the pull is retried only for the duration of the triggering block’s round.
Workers stream batches continuously, sized at a few hundred to a few thousand transactions, around 500 KB. Most batches reach other validators before the primary block that references them, which shortens the time to sign and keeps the network busy while validators wait for 2f+12f+12f+1 primary blocks.
The authors estimate when the primary would become the bottleneck. A batch of 1,000 transactions of 512 bytes is 512 KB, while its entry in a primary block is a 32-byte hash plus 8 bytes of worker ID, 40 bytes in total. By their arithmetic, about 12,000 workers would be needed before the primary handles data volumes comparable to a single worker. They report never observing the primary as a bottleneck and leave accumulators like Merkle roots to future work.
Tusk: consensus read off the DAGTusk starts from DAG-Rider (Keidar et al., 2021), inherits its safety argument, and modifies it for implementation and lower common-case latency. Validators run Narwhal and additionally place in each block a share of a distributed perfect random coin, built from an adaptively secure threshold signature scheme whose key setup can itself be done under asynchrony. Each validator then interprets its own local DAG to derive the total order. No consensus message is ever sent.
The DAG is divided into waves of three consecutive rounds. In the first round, validators propose by creating blocks. In the second, they vote by referencing first-round blocks. In the third, they reveal coin shares that retroactively elect one first-round block as the wave’s leader. As an optimization, the third round of one wave doubles as the first round of the next. A validator commits the elected leader if, in its local view, at least f+1f+1f+1 second-round blocks reference it.
Different validators may see different local DAGs, so one may commit a leader that another skips. To reconcile, after committing the leader of wave www, a validator walks back to the last wave w′w'w′ where it committed. For each wave in between, from latest to earliest, if there is a path from the current candidate to that wave’s leader, the earlier leader is ordered first and becomes the new candidate. Each leader’s causal history is then ordered by a fixed deterministic rule.
Figure 6 is the paper’s example, with two waves, four validators and f=1f=1f=1. Columns are rounds and squares are blocks. The leader L1L_1L1​ of wave 1, elected at round 3, has fewer than f+1f+1f+1 references in round 2 and is not committed at that point. The leader L2L_2L2​ of wave 2, elected at round 5, has f+1=2f+1 = 2f+1=2 references in round 4 and commits. Because a path exists from L2L_2L2​ to L1L_1L1​, L1L_1L1​ is ordered first, followed by L2L_2L2​, each with its causal sub-DAG.
Figure 6. Example of commit rule in Tusk. Every odd round has a coin value that selects a leader of round r−2r-2r−2. If the leader has less than f+1f+1f+1 support (red) they are ignored, otherwise (blue) the algorithm searches the causal DAG to commit all preceding leaders (including red) and totally orders the rest of the DAG afterward.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 5 (© the authors) The thick lines carry the argument. The red line out of L1L_1L1​ reaches a single block of round 2, so L1L_1L1​ has one vote where it needs two. The two blue lines are the votes for L2L_2L2​ from round 4. The red line then continues from that round-2 block to L2L_2L2​, and this is the path that puts L1L_1L1​ into the order ahead of L2L_2L2​. The dashed arrows are the coin: the value revealed in round 3 selects the fourth validator’s block of round 1, and the value revealed in round 5 selects the third validator’s block of round 3.
Why every honest validator commits the same leadersSafety rests on two lemmas.
Lemma 1: if an honest validator commits leader block bbb in wave iii, then any leader block b′b'b′ committed by any honest validator vvv in a later wave has a path to bbb in vvv’s local DAG.
The reason is quorum intersection. Committing bbb requires f+1f+1f+1 second-round blocks linking to it. Every block in the next round links to 2f+12f+12f+1 blocks of the round before, and any set of 2f+12f+12f+1 blocks out of at most 3f+13f+13f+1 must intersect any set of f+1f+1f+1. So every block in the first round of wave i+1i+1i+1 has a path to bbb, and by induction so does every block in every later round.
Lemma 2: any two honest validators commit the same sequence of block leaders.
The appendix derives it from Lemma A.6: if an honest validator commits bbb before b′b'b′, no honest validator commits b′b'b′ without first committing bbb. Otherwise, one validator’s order implies there is no path between the two leaders, contradicting Lemma 1. Combined with Narwhal’s Containment property, which ensures every validator sees the same causal history behind each leader, all honest validators agree on the total order of the DAG’s blocks.
Why Tusk terminates, and how fastLiveness follows the pattern of the VABA protocol (Abraham et al., 2019): force the adversary to fix a communication schedule, then use a perfect shared coin so that a useful outcome is selected with constant probability.
Lemma 3: for every wave, at least f+1f+1f+1 blocks in its first round satisfy the commit rule.
The proof is a counting argument. Take any 2f+12f+12f+1 second-round blocks. Each references 2f+12f+12f+1 first-round blocks, for a total of
(2f+1)(2f+1)=4f2+4f+1 (2f+1)(2f+1) = 4f^2 + 4f + 1 (2f+1)(2f+1)=4f2+4f+1links. There are at most 3f+13f+13f+1 first-round blocks. Even if each of them receives fff links, that uses f(3f+1)f(3f+1)f(3f+1), leaving
4f2+4f+1−f(3f+1)=f2+3f+1 4f^2 + 4f + 1 - f(3f+1) = f^2 + 3f + 1 4f2+4f+1−f(3f+1)=f2+3f+1links. A block can receive at most 2f+12f+12f+1 links, so at most f+1f+1f+1 beyond the baseline fff. The number of blocks with at least f+1f+1f+1 links is therefore at least
f2+3f+1f+1≥f+1. \frac{f^2 + 3f + 1}{f+1} \ge f+1. f+1f2+3f+1​≥f+1.The coin is revealed only in the third round, after the first two rounds, and therefore these f+1f+1f+1 committable blocks, are already fixed. The adversary cannot steer the election away from them. Each wave therefore commits with probability at least f+13f+1>13\frac{f+1}{3f+1} > \frac{1}{3}3f+1f+1​>31​, even with full adversarial control of the network.
Lemma 4: in expectation, Tusk commits a block leader every 7 rounds under an asynchronous adversary. With success probability at least 1/3, a commit happens every 3 waves in expectation, and with three-round waves that share a round, the paper arrives at 7 rounds.
Lemma 5: in networks with random message delays, each block in the DAG is committed in 4.5 rounds in expectation. Here each second-round block references the leader independently with probability at least 2f+13f+1≥23\frac{2f+1}{3f+1} \ge \frac{2}{3}3f+12f+1​≥32​. For f=1f=1f=1, the worst case, the probability that at least 2 of 3 voters reference the leader is 827+1227≈0.74\frac{8}{27} + \frac{12}{27} \approx 0.74278​+2712​≈0.74, so the commit probability per wave is at least 0.74. For comparison, DAG-Rider’s four-round waves give 5.5 rounds per block in the common case.
Because neither the coin nor the commit logic adds messages, Tusk has the same theoretical throughput as Narwhal itself.
What the evaluation shows: the mempool sets throughput, consensus sets latencyThe evaluation has four claims to support: Narwhal beats both a gossip mempool and plain batching, adding workers raises throughput linearly, Tusk keeps its throughput as the committee grows, and all of this survives faults. Sections 7.1 to 7.3 of the paper answer with one experiment each.
Implementation and testbedThe validator is written in Rust using Tokio for asynchronous networking, ed25519-dalek for signatures and RocksDB for persistence, in about 4,000 lines plus 2,000 lines of tests. Messages are held in memory and resent over persistent TCP connections that are re-established on failure, until the protocol logic decides they are no longer needed, which bounds memory spent on unreachable peers. For comparison the authors implement HotStuff themselves, adding persistent storage and a pacemaker following the LibraBFT specification, in two versions: Baseline-HS with a gossip mempool and Batched-HS as described earlier.
Experiments run on AWS m5.8xlarge instances, each with 10 Gbps of bandwidth, 32 virtual CPUs and 128 GB of memory, spread across five regions: N. Virginia, N. California, Sydney, Stockholm and Tokyo. The baseline parameters are 4 validators with one worker each, 500 KB batches, 1 KB blocks, 512-byte transactions, and one benchmark client per worker submitting at a fixed rate for 5 minutes. Each point in the graphs is the average of 2 runs, with error bars of one standard deviation. Latency is the time from a client submitting a transaction to the leader that proposed it committing it.
One worker per validatorThe first experiment is the head-to-head comparison: a WAN, no faults, one worker collocated with each primary, and committees of 10, 20 and 50 validators (10 and 20 for Baseline-HS). Figure 7 plots it. The horizontal axis is throughput and the vertical axis is latency, and each point is one input rate. Color is the system: green for Tusk, blue for Narwhal-HS, orange for Batched-HS, red for Baseline-HS. Line style is the committee: solid for 10 validators, dashed for 20, dotted for 50. A curve runs flat while the system keeps up with the load and turns upward where it saturates, so the place to look is where each curve bends. Baseline-HS is the red sliver against the left edge.
Figure 7. Comparative throughput-latency performance for the novel Narwhal-HotStuff, Tusk, batched-HotStuff and the baseline HotStuff. WAN measurements with 10, 20, and 50 validators, using 1 worker collocated with the primary. No validator faults, 500KB max. block size and 512B transaction size.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 6 (© the authors) Table 1 collects the numbers the paper states for this experiment.
Table 1. Peak throughput and latency without faults, one worker per validator.
System Peak throughput Latency Baseline-HS never above 1,800 tx/s about 1 s Batched-HS 70,000 tx/s with 10 validators, up to 50,000 with 20 about 2 s before saturation Narwhal-HS 140,000 tx/s below 2 s Tusk 170,000 tx/s with 50 validators about 3 s at every committee size The abstract and the conclusion quote slightly lower numbers for the last two rows, over 130,000 tx/s for Narwhal-HS and 160,000 for Tusk, and the conclusion ties the first to the 50-validator deployment.
The Baseline-HS number looks low until it is set next to the ones the authors cite: 3,500 tx/s for HotStuff on a LAN and around 500 tx/s for LibraBFT. Batched-HS is the instructive row. It is the same consensus code with dissemination taken off the critical path, and the authors put the gain at almost 20x. Its throughput falls as the committee grows. Narwhal-HS goes the other way, which the authors attribute to the worker implementation not using each machine’s network, disk and CPU fully, so that more validators multiplex those resources better.
The two Narwhal systems differ mainly in latency, which is what the paper’s hypothesis predicts: the mempool determines throughput and the consensus on top determines how long a transaction waits. Tusk’s 3 seconds is more than its theoretical 4.5 rounds would suggest. The authors give two reasons. The implementation puts transactions in the blocks of every round, not only a wave’s first round, which adds half a round in expectation. And synchronization is deliberately conservative, so a validator takes a little longer to collect the full causal history before it can order.
Scaling out with workersFor the scale-out experiment every worker and every primary gets its own instance, so a validator with 4 workers is 5 machines. Workers sit in the same data center as their primary, and the 4 validators are spread over the five regions. The runs use 4, 7 and 10 workers per validator, with batches of 1,000 transactions. Figure 8 reports it in two plots.
Figure 8. Tusk and HS with Narwhal latency-throughput graph for 4 validators and different number of workers. The transaction and batch sizes are respectively set to 512B and 1,000 transactions.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 7 (© the authors) The upper plot has the axes of Figure 7, with green for Tusk and blue for Narwhal-HS, and solid, dashed and dotted lines for 4, 7 and 10 workers. The bends come in three groups, one per worker count, while the flat parts stay at the same height. In the paper’s words, configurations with more workers saturate later at the same latency, which they take as proof that the primary is far from saturated even with 10 workers feeding it hashes. The lower plot has workers per validator on the horizontal axis and throughput on the vertical, in tx/s on the left and MB/s on the right. It fixes a latency bound of 5 seconds (solid lines) or 3 seconds (dashed) and reports the highest throughput that stays under it. The lines are close to straight: the points fall close to the number of workers times the throughput of one worker. The abstract summarizes this as linear growth to 600,000 tx/s with no latency increase, and the introduction as over 500,000 tx/s at under 3.5 seconds. Read off the lower plot, the 10-worker points sit between 500,000 and 600,000 tx/s, and a single worker in this 4-validator setup delivers about 50,000.
Crash faultsThe fault experiment repeats the comparison of all four systems with 10 validators and 1 or 3 of them crashed, 3 being the most that 10 can tolerate. Figure 9 has the same axes and colors as Figure 7, with the latency axis now reaching 40 seconds. Solid lines are runs with one fault and dashed lines runs with three. The red and orange curves stay against the left edge and climb; the green and blue ones still extend to the right.
Figure 9. Comparative throughput-latency under faults. WAN measurements with 10 validators, using 1 worker collocated with the primary. One and three faults, 500KB max. block size and 512B transaction size.Danezis et al., Narwhal and Tusk, EuroSys ’22, Figure 8 (© the authors) With three faults, Baseline-HS throughput drops 5x from an already low 800 tx/s and its latency rises 40x. Batched-HS drops 30x, from 70,000 to 2,500 tx/s, with latency up 10x. The paper puts the latency of both at 35 to 40 seconds. Table 2 gives the latency of the two Narwhal systems.
Table 2. Latency of the Narwhal-based systems with 1 and 3 of 10 validators crashed.
System Latency, 1 fault Latency, 3 faults Tusk under 4 s under 6 s Narwhal-HS under 7 s about 10 s Tusk and Narwhal-HS keep a good level of throughput, and the authors attribute most of the loss to the missing capacity of the crashed machines. The text gives no number; in Figure 9 the one-fault curves run to about 120,000 tx/s and the three-fault curves stop short of 80,000. Tusk’s latency grows because the coin elects an absent leader more often. Narwhal-HS is slower than Tusk, as the paper’s theoretical comparison predicts for a leader-based protocol, and still far ahead of the other HotStuff variants. The authors conjecture two causes: consensus over Narwhal has very little data to carry, and the first successful commit picks up a large fraction of recent transactions thanks to 2/3-Causality.
All of these are crash faults. The paper notes that evaluating BFT protocols in the presence of Byzantine faults is still an open research question.
How the paper positions itselfAgainst Mir-BFT (Stathakopoulou et al., 2019), which reaches about 80,000 tx/s under 2 seconds for 20 WAN validators and falls to zero throughput for up to 50 seconds after faults, the authors report Tusk with one worker slightly higher at double the latency, and about 9x higher with multiple workers. Among asynchronous protocols, they cite Dumbo2 at 5,000 tx/s within 5 seconds on 8 WAN nodes and claim a 20x speedup.
Relative to DAG-Rider, Tusk replaces classic reliable broadcast with the pull-based scheme, shortens the commit rule, and removes weak links. DAG-Rider uses weak links to reference older blocks for block-level fairness, which forces storing every block ever received. Tusk instead re-injects transactions from collected blocks, settling for transaction-level fairness. The authors estimate DAG-Rider itself would take under 200 lines on top of Narwhal. They contrast Narwhal with Hashgraph, which lacks a layered threshold-clock structure and relies on local coins, and with Blockmania (Danezis and Hrycyszyn, 2018), neither of which separates availability from consensus.
The paper lists its own limitations. Slow validators are indistinguishable from faulty ones, so distant but correct validators may see their transactions committed late. Clients must resubmit transactions a faulty validator drops; sending to f+1f+1f+1 validators would divide bandwidth by O(n)O(n)O(n), so the authors suggest a small fixed number. Spreading data across workers burdens the execution engine and light clients, which must locate transactions across machines. And the throughput only matters if an execution engine can keep up, which the authors defer to future work. Their concluding claim is that the main cost of large-scale blockchain protocols is reliable transaction dissemination rather than consensus, and that dissemination without global sequencing is embarrassingly parallel.
My takeThe most convincing result in this paper belongs to Batched-HS. The same HotStuff goes from 1,800 to 70,000 tx/s once the leader proposes hashes, and falls back to 2,500 when three of ten validators crash. Everything Narwhal adds, the certificates and the rounds, exists to close that second gap, and the fault experiment shows that it does.
The idea transfers to a permissioned ordering service only in part. In the BFT orderer we built for Fabric, a follower verifies every transaction in the leader’s proposal before it votes. Narwhal’s validity conditions cover the creator’s signature, the round and the certificates. They say nothing about what is inside a batch. So the mempool certifies the availability of data nobody has validated, and filtering moves to an execution layer the paper leaves out.
The headline numbers also matter less for that setting than they look. A consortium that needs a few thousand transactions per second gains nothing from 130,000, and it pays in latency: about 1 second for Baseline-HS at low load, under 2 for Narwhal-HS, about 3 for Tusk. What it would be buying is the fault behavior.
That is where the evaluation is thinnest. It tests crashes and nothing else, and the authors say so. The adversary this design should worry about stays up, signs for batches, and is slow or selective when asked to serve them. The pull path is argued to need O(1)O(1)O(1) requests on average and O(n)O(n)O(n) under attack, and it is never measured. Each point averages two five-minute runs. The scale-out result uses 4 validators with workers in the primary’s data center, and the comparisons with Mir-BFT and Dumbo2 use numbers reported in other papers.
Operationally, “add workers” is a bigger ask than it sounds. Ten workers and a primary are eleven machines, and every organization in the committee has to run that cluster. The paper treats a validator as either correct or faulty. It does not say what happens when one worker loses its disk after the primary has signed for the batches on it. Garbage collection bounds memory, not storage: old rounds go to a store the paper describes as a CDN or S3 and does not evaluate. At 600,000 tx/s of 512-byte transactions each validator’s store grows by about 300 MB every second.
Before adopting it I would want the fault experiments rerun with a validator that withholds batches. I would want to know how a validator that was offline past the garbage collection round catches up. And I would ask what a membership change costs, because the paper works with a fixed committee and Tusk’s coin depends on a threshold key setup.
Narwhal and Tusk: A DAG-based Mempool and Efficient BFT Consensus. George Danezis, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino, Alexander Spiegelman. EuroSys '22, 2022.
summary: For most of the last decade, work on fast Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus has focused on one number: message complexity, meaning how many protocol messages the validators exchange per decision. HotStuff (Yin et al., 2019) brought that number down to linear in the partially synchronous setting by routing all votes through a leader. The paper by Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino and Spiegelman, published at EuroSys 2022, argues that this target misses where the cost actually sits in a real ledger. The expensive part is not agreeing on an order. It is moving the transactions themselves to every validator, reliably.
title: Narwhal and Tusk: Moving the Bottleneck Out of BFT Consensus

Fabric’s ordering service receives endorsed transactions from clients and emits a stream of blocks. When we wrote this paper the latest release, v2.3, ran it on Raft, which tolerates crashes and nothing worse. The paper describes how my co-authors and I made Fabric Byzantine fault-tolerant end to end: a consensus library in Go, based on the BFT-SMaRt protocol, and the changes to the orderer, the peer and the client that had to come with it.
Why the 2018 attempt was not adoptedIn 2018 Sousa et al. took the Kafka-based ordering service of Fabric v1.1 and replaced Kafka with a cluster of BFT-SMaRt servers. The proof of concept showed promising performance and was still not adopted by the community.
It was two processes in two languages, a Go front end and a Java BFT server. The code that wrapped the BFT-SMaRt core did not include Fabric’s membership service provider, so the cluster’s signatures were not compliant with Fabric’s and its identities were not part of Fabric’s configuration. Blocks carried the signature of a single front-end orderer, so nobody looking at a block could be convinced that a BFT service had produced it. And a follower could not validate the leader’s proposal against Fabric’s semantics without pulling in a significant amount of Fabric’s code.
Our candidates were BFT-SMaRt and PBFT, and we soon realized that rewriting the Java or C implementation in Go would not be enough.
Quorums, Raft against PBFTLoosely speaking, a crash fault tolerant protocol like Raft needs a simple majority, and a Byzantine fault tolerant one like PBFT needs two thirds. With NNN nodes and a quorum of size QQQ:
QCFT=12NQBFT=23NF=N−Q Q_{\mathrm{CFT}} = \tfrac{1}{2}N \qquad Q_{\mathrm{BFT}} = \tfrac{2}{3}N \qquad F = N - Q QCFT​=21​NQBFT​=32​NF=N−QSo the BFT cluster needs more replicas to survive the same number of faults FFF. In our evaluation, resilience to two faults takes 7 BFT nodes against 5 for Raft. PBFT also runs three communication rounds where Raft runs two, and it needs cryptography.
A library that calls back into FabricThe library is embedded in the ordering node’s process, as the Raft library is. The difference is the interface. In the monolithic BFT-SMaRt cluster the flow starts with submit and ends with deliver. Ours adds functions that the application implements and the library calls while the protocol runs.
Figure 1. The BFT ordering service node. The consensus library is in the middle, and validation, block assembly and signing are Fabric’s.Barger, Manevich, Meir and Tock, arXiv:2107.06922 , Fig. 1 (CC BY 4.0) The leader batches incoming transactions and calls Assemble, and Fabric decides how the batch becomes a block. A configuration transaction, for instance, must sit in a block by itself. A follower that receives the proposal calls VerifyProposal, because the leader may be malicious. Fabric checks that the block is correctly numbered, that its header contains the hash of the previous block, and that every transaction in it is valid. In the commit phase each node calls SignProposal and sends the signature as part of its COMMIT message.

Collecting the signatures during the commit phase keeps the protocol at three rounds, where the 2018 design needed four, and it lets an observer of a single block check that the ordering service agreed on it.
Clients submit to all nodes, not only to the leader. If a request is not included in a proposal after a first timeout, every non-faulty follower forwards it to the leader. After a second timeout they initiate a view change. The first step protects against a malicious client that sends only to followers to force a view change, the second against a faulty leader.
Peers and clients had to change tooFabric’s default policy accepts a block with a single signature from a node of any organization in the ordering service consortium. We implemented a validation policy that requires signatures from QQQ out of NNN nodes of the consenter set defined in the last channel configuration transaction, and it is updated every time that set changes.
Blocks signed this way cannot be forged, but a peer that receives its blocks from a single orderer can still be censored. Asking F+1F+1F+1 orderers for the full stream would work and is expensive. Instead the peer requests full blocks from one randomly selected orderer and a stream of only headers and metadata from all the rest. If FFF or more of those streams are ahead of the full block stream for more than a threshold period, the peer suspects the orderer of censorship and replaces it. On the client side we modified the Fabric Java SDK to submit every transaction to all the orderers.
What it costs in throughputWe compared it with the Raft ordering service from Fabric v2.3, using transactions of about 4KB. With 1000 transactions per block and resilience to two faults, the BFT service did 2,500 tx/sec in a LAN against 13,000 for Raft, which is 20%. With the servers in ten data centers across the globe it did 1,200 against 3,000, which is 40%.
We attribute the gap mainly to two things: the cryptographic computations required in all BFT protocols, and the lack of pipelining in the BFT-SMaRt protocol. Our leader starts consensus on a block only after the previous one has been committed. We chose BFT-SMaRt for that simplicity. With a single proposal from a given leader at any point in time the view change sub-protocol is much simpler, and that increases our confidence in the correctness of the implementation. These numbers are for a single channel, and a Fabric network can scale horizontally by adding channels.
My takeIf I had to keep one thing from this paper it would be the interface, not the protocol. Letting the application assemble, verify and sign the proposal while consensus runs is what made a BFT orderer fit into Fabric at all, and it would work just as well with a different protocol underneath.
We gave up pipelining on purpose. One proposal per leader at a time keeps the view change simple enough that I trust the implementation, and the price is plain in the numbers: 20% of Raft in a LAN, 40% in a WAN. I would make the same trade again for a first production-grade BFT orderer. I would not claim it is the right trade forever.
The comparison with Raft is honest about what it measures: 7 nodes against 5, 4KB transactions, a single channel. It says little about the workloads where most Fabric networks sit, well below either ceiling. For those the question is not how fast but what it costs to operate seven orderers across organizations.
The part I would want tested harder is the block delivery on the peer. Detecting censorship by comparing header streams against one full stream rests on a threshold period, and the paper does not say how to choose it or how the peer behaves when the network, not the orderer, is slow.
What the paper understates is how much of the effort was outside consensus. The signature policy on the peer, the delivery service and the SDK change are each small on the page, and without any one of them the system is not Byzantine fault-tolerant end to end.

summary: Fabric’s ordering service receives endorsed transactions from clients and emits a stream of blocks. When we wrote this paper the latest release, v2.3, ran it on Raft, which tolerates crashes and nothing worse. The paper describes how my co-authors and I made Fabric Byzantine fault-tolerant end to end: a consensus library in Go, based on the BFT-SMaRt protocol, and the changes to the orderer, the peer and the client that had to come with it.
